transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
New York prosecutors are reopening a criminal investigation into an alleged sexual assault
involving students at Cornell University.
A former student says she was drugged and gang-raped at the school in 2024.
At the time, no criminal charges were filed.
Two weeks ago, she filed suit with new allegations against Cornell and seven male students.
NPR's Brian Mann has been speaking with women in the Cornell community.
I spoke with Olympia Hall.
She's a current Cornell student.
She's co-president of the Sexual Assault Prevention and Safety Club on campus.
She says Cornell has tried to improve campus safety, but she says she still sometimes feel
vulnerable.
And she told me fraternities on campus hold a lot of sway over students' social life.
That is a cultural aspect that creates a lot of power dynamics that are uncomfortable and
lead young men to potentially not think about their actions.
NPR's Brian Mann brought us that story from Ithaca, New York.
President Trump is meeting with AI leaders at the White House this afternoon, a day after
the big tech company OpenAI said it is scrapping the release of its newest AI model after it
failed to meet company internal testing standards.
We have more from NPR's John Ruich.
The company had been planning to release the model, called GPT-6.1 Astra, in the coming
days.
But it's decided to scrap the release.
Sachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI, said, "It didn't quite meet the bar in testing
and fell short in terms of communication with the user about the work it's done."
He told the Wall Street Journal it performed poorly on alignment, the term AI developers
use for how well a model sticks to what people want, rather than going off script.
In an emailed statement, Jain says, "When shipping new models to users, OpenAI has an
extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment.
The company says it has other new models coming soon."
John Ruich, NPR News.
Israeli settlers stormed a Palestinian village in the Israeli-occupied West Bank overnight.
The group attacked a Palestinian family after an Israeli court ordered they be allowed to
return home and PR's Kat Lonstorf is more.
More than 100 violent Israeli settlers attacked the village of Jalud, setting fire to buildings
and vehicles and throwing stones, according to the Israeli military.
The attack happened as Israeli security forces were attempting to escort a Palestinian family
back to their home.
That family had been forced to leave their home about two months ago, due to continuous
harassment by Israeli settlers, according to an Israeli court order.
Instead, Israeli settlers set fire to the home and the family fled again.
Two of the settlers were arrested and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned
the attack.
Netanyahu recently downplayed such violence in a speech at the UN.
The UN has tracked about 200 settler attacks per month in 2026.
Kat Lonstorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
It's NPR News.
The attorney of a Massachusetts woman who killed her three young children in 2023 was back
in court today for the first time since a judge declared a mistrial earlier this month
when the jury was deadlocked over whether to hold Lindsay Clancy criminally responsible.
Kevin Redington pushed for Clancy's acquittal, arguing today that his client was psychotic
and delusional at the time of her children's death.
The prosecution says Clancy knew exactly what she was doing and dismissed the defense's
argument as, quote, laughable.
Today, the judge made no decision.
Hurricane Polo made landfall in Baja, California as a category two this morning and brought
the threat of flash floods and destructive winds of up to 110 miles per hour.
The National Hurricane Center projects the storm could deliver heavy rain to parts of
the southwestern U.S. later this week.
This year's MacArthur Fellows have just been announced and Piazzari Daniel has details.
The recipients include a bioengineer creating nanotechnologies to improve vaccines and drug
delivery, a climate researcher examining polar sea ice and global change, and a public artist
converting neglected spaces into visual work rooted in community.
A couple of the winners sit at the intersection of science and justice.
Like Texas State University forensic anthropologist Kate Spradley, she's on a lifelong mission
to help identify the buried remains of hundreds of migrants who've died after making the southern
border crossing.
Everyone should have dignity and death.
Each MacArthur Fellow receives $800,000 over five years, no strings attached.
For NPR News, I'm Ari Daniel.

topics.text: New York prosecutors reopen criminal investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University
OpenAI scraps release of GPT-6.1 Astra model after failing internal safety testing standards
Israeli settlers attack Palestinian village of Jalud, setting fires as family returns home
Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case; prosecution and defense dispute her criminal responsibility
Hurricane Polo makes landfall in Baja California as Category 2 storm with destructive winds
MacArthur Fellows announced including forensic anthropologist Kate Spradley identifying migrant remains at border
